strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: precision limitations of VLAs due to greedy/single-inference decoding, without requiring external trained verifiers.
The proposed condition-masking distribution as a reference for KL-divergence-based confidence is a reasonably novel and intuitive idea adapted from self-certainty measures in LLM literature.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO) and real-world Franka robot experiments (ID and OOD tasks), spanning two different VLA architectures (π0-FAST and OpenVLA).

Thorough ablation studies covering inference strategy, number of candidates, masking variants, joint training effect, regularization temperature, and token aggregation strategy, providing useful insight into design choices.
Practical engineering contribution via single-prefill deployment strategy that substantially reduces inference latency overhead from parallel sampling.
Strong performance gains reported in low-data regimes (e.g., 168% relative improvement with 30 demonstrations on RoboCasa pick-and-place), which is a meaningful practical setting.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the external-verifier baselines that motivate the paper (Nakamoto et al. 2024's value-guided approach, Kwok et al. 2025's RoboMonkey); the paper only discusses them conceptually in related work, leaving the central claim of superiority over verifier-based TTS unvalidated empirically.

The strongest results throughout the paper rely on MG-Select* (with the proposed joint training/fine-tuning strategy), which requires additional training on augmented condition-masking data — this partially undermines the paper's core "no additional training" selling point versus verifier-based methods, since joint training itself is non-trivial additional training overhead.

Results on LIBERO with OpenVLA are inconsistent: performance decreases on LIBERO-Spatial (85.2→81.7) and LIBERO-Goal (75.5→73.6), which is not adequately discussed or explained, weakening the claim of general effectiveness across architectures.

The method requires an extensive per-dataset hyperparameter search (temperature τ, N, masking variant, regularization temperature ranges given in Appendix A.3), raising concerns about practical deployability and the robustness/generality of a supposedly "verifier-free" and simple approach.

Real-world evaluation trial counts are relatively small (24 trials for ID, 16 for OOD tasks per condition), and no variance/confidence intervals are reported for these results, limiting statistical confidence in the reported real-world gains.

The token aggregation strategy (e.g., "first 5 tokens" working best) appears heuristic and closely tied to the specific FAST tokenizer structure, raising questions about generalizability to other action tokenization schemes or continuous-action (diffusion-based) VLAs, which are not evaluated at all despite being discussed in related work.

Limited theoretical grounding for why the condition-masking distribution is a principled 'uncertainty-aware' reference beyond empirical validation; the explanation is largely post-hoc and intuition-based rather than rigorously justified.

strengths: Novel and intuitive idea: using condition-masked (state/language dropout) distributions as an internal, verifier-free reference for KL-divergence-based confidence scoring in autoregressive VLAs, motivated by the observation that raw likelihood-based selection fails due to overly peaked action distributions.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide range of simulated benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN) and real-world robot experiments (Franka arm, ID and OOD tasks), demonstrating fairly consistent improvements over greedy decoding baselines.
Method is shown to generalize across multiple VLA architectures and scales (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA), suggesting the approach is not tied to a specific backbone.

Thorough ablation studies covering nearly every design choice: masking variant, number of candidates, aggregation strategy, dropout ratio, regularization temperature, and comparison to uniform-KL and likelihood-based baselines, which helps substantiate the design decisions.
Practical engineering contribution via the single-prefill deployment strategy that substantially reduces inference latency overhead from parallel sampling.
Direct comparison against an external-verifier baseline (RoboMonkey) shows competitive accuracy with lower latency and no extra verifier module, strengthening the core motivating claim.
Reasonably good reproducibility support via detailed implementation/hyperparameter appendices.
weaknesses: The framework requires an extensive per-dataset/per-task hyperparameter search (temperature, N, masking variant, regularization temperature over fairly large grids) to find the best configuration, which somewhat undercuts the 'no additional training or tuning burden' narrative and raises concerns about practical deployability and overfitting to test benchmarks.

The strongest results consistently depend on the proposed joint training strategy (MG-Select*), meaning the purely test-time, training-free variant (MG-Select) is often only a modest improvement; this weakens the 'verifier-free/training-free' framing as a central selling point.

Absolute success rates remain quite low in several settings (e.g., RoboCasa pick-and-place around 14–47%), so while relative gains are large, the practical precision problem is only partially mitigated.

Statistical rigor is limited: only 3 random seeds are used, no variance/error bars are reported for most tables, and real-world trial counts are small (16–24 trials), limiting confidence in the significance of reported gains, especially smaller ones (e.g., LIBERO-Goal shows slight regressions with MG-Select for both architectures).

The theoretical justification in Appendix E is a fairly standard/trivial derivation (entropy of a softmax increases with temperature) and does not provide deep insight into why condition-masking specifically yields a good confidence reference beyond the empirical ablations.

The comparison to RoboMonkey removes its majority-voting and Gaussian-perturbation components for a 'fair' comparison, which may not represent RoboMonkey's full intended pipeline and could bias the comparison in MG-Select's favor.

The method is developed and validated only for autoregressive/token-based VLAs; applicability to increasingly common diffusion/flow-based action experts (e.g., π0 without FAST tokenization, GR00T) is not discussed or evaluated, limiting generality claims.

The aggregation strategy (truncating to first K tokens) appears somewhat heuristic and dataset-specific (first 5 for RoboCasa/LIBERO, first 1 optimal for SIMPLER-WidowX per appendix), suggesting fragility that requires further tuning per domain rather than a principled, transferable rule.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple simulation benchmarks (RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN) and real-world Franka experiments, plus multiple base architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA), which lends some breadth to the claims.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies covering temperature, number of candidates, masking variants, dropout ratio, and token-aggregation strategy.
An efficient single-prefill deployment strategy is proposed and shown to substantially reduce the latency overhead of Best-of-N sampling, addressing a real practical concern.
A direct comparison against an external-verifier baseline (RoboMonkey) is included, which is a fair and informative addition.
Simple theoretical justification connecting temperature scaling of the masked reference distribution to entropy is provided (though of limited depth).
weaknesses: The paper's central claim of being 'verifier-free' and requiring 'no additional training' is undercut by the fact that the strongest results throughout the paper (MG-Select*) rely on the proposed joint fine-tuning strategy, which is itself an additional training procedure; the truly training-free variant (MG-Select) yields much smaller gains (e.g., Table 5(d): 22.6 vs 31.0 PnP), making the framing in the abstract/intro somewhat misleading.

The method requires an extensive, largely per-dataset hyperparameter search (sampling temperature, N, masking variant among text/state/both, regularization temperature over 7 values) as stated in Appendix A.3, with the 'best result for each policy' reported; this raises concerns about practical usability and whether results generalize without dataset-specific oracle tuning on test performance.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core idea of using KL-to-a-perturbed-reference-distribution as a self-certainty confidence score is directly adapted from existing LLM self-certainty/verifier-free TTS work (Kang et al. 2025); the main contribution is the masking-based construction of the reference distribution for the VLA setting, which is a relatively straightforward extension.

In the direct comparison to the external-verifier baseline (Table 14), RoboMonkey actually achieves a slightly higher average success rate than MG-Select* (50.7 vs 50.3) and wins on 2 of 4 tasks, which weakens the argument that a verifier-free approach can match or beat verifier-based methods in accuracy (the benefit is really confined to latency).

Reported gains are inconsistent across some settings — e.g., LIBERO-Goal success drops slightly with π0-FAST+MG-Select* (95.6→94.5) and OpenVLA LIBERO-Spatial drops slightly (85.0→84.8) — and the failure-case analysis in Appendix G acknowledges the method can introduce unnecessary stochasticity on simple tasks, which is not sufficiently addressed in the main results discussion.

Absolute performance on the headline RoboCasa pick-and-place task remains low (e.g., 31.0% at 100 demos, 46.9% at 300 demos), so while relative improvements are large (e.g., 168%), the practical significance of the gains for real deployment is still limited.

Only 3 random seeds are used and no variance/confidence intervals are reported for success rates, making it harder to assess the statistical robustness of the (often modest, single-digit) percentage-point improvements.

The token-aggregation strategy (truncating to first 5 tokens) is heuristic and explicitly tied to the specific frequency-ordering property of the FAST tokenizer, limiting the generality of this design choice to other tokenization schemes; the optimal truncation length even differs between benchmarks (first 1 for SIMPLER-WidowX vs first 5 for RoboCasa), further suggesting a lack of a principled, transferable rule.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across many benchmarks: RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world Franka experiments, plus multiple base architectures (π0-FAST, OpenVLA, MiniVLA), giving good evidence of generality.

Addresses a practical and important problem (precision limitations of greedy decoding in VLAs) with a genuinely verifier-free approach, removing the need for costly external reward models used in prior work (Nakamoto et al., Kwok et al.).
Thorough ablation studies (masking variant, temperature, aggregation strategy, dropout ratio, number of candidates) that help explain design choices and provide useful insight for practitioners.
Practical systems contribution: the single-prefill deployment strategy meaningfully reduces the added latency of Best-of-N sampling, making the method more deployable.
Direct comparison against an external-verifier baseline (RoboMonkey) shows the proposed method achieves comparable performance at substantially lower latency and without training a separate verifier.
Real-world experiments (in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks) with qualitative visualizations provide convincing evidence beyond simulation.
weaknesses: The optimal masking variant (text/state/both) and aggregation window (first-K tokens) both require per-dataset/per-domain hyperparameter search, which somewhat undercuts the paper's framing of being training/tuning-free and raises questions about generalization to genuinely novel domains without such tuning.

Absolute performance in several settings remains low (e.g., 14.2%-46.9% on RoboCasa pick-and-place), so while relative improvements are large, practical utility for high-precision tasks is still limited.

In the head-to-head comparison with RoboMonkey (external verifier), the verifier-based method still slightly outperforms MG-Select in average success rate (50.7 vs 50.3), which weakens the central claim that verifier-free selection can match verifier-based methods, though efficiency gains are a valid selling point.

Some inconsistent reporting conventions between MG-Select and MG-Select* across tables (e.g., real-world OOD table reports MG-Select while ID table reports MG-Select*) makes it harder to disentangle the contribution of joint training vs. test-time selection alone in some settings.

The theoretical derivation in Appendix E is a fairly standard/well-known result (entropy of a softmax distribution increases with temperature) and does not provide deep new insight specific to VLAs or the proposed method.

No variance/standard deviation is reported in the main result tables despite averaging over 3 seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported gains, especially in low-demonstration regimes where variance is likely high.

The method still incurs additional inference cost (N forward passes) relative to greedy decoding, and although single-prefill mitigates this, latency still increases notably at larger N (e.g., 2x at N=64), constraining real-time deployment.

LIBERO results show mixed effects on individual task suites (e.g., LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal slightly decrease with MG-Select for OpenVLA and π0-FAST respectively), suggesting the method is not uniformly beneficial and can sometimes hurt tasks where the base policy is already near-optimal, as acknowledged in the failure case analysis.
